sources.note: Read 2026-11-17: the record page (title, report number, date; the change notices add intramuscular injection, vaccination in a public health emergency and nasal swab collection at EMT and above) and the PDF's skill tables through a summarizing fetch whose table columns were partly unclear, so placement was checked against the course's own reading (backend/supabase/seed/labs/ems-sources.ts, 2026-11-09) and REQ-241's reading (2026-11-11). EMR: oxygen, BVM, naloxone (intranasal or auto-injector), unit-dose hazmat antidote auto-injectors, tourniquet, wound packing, emergency moves, manual stabilization; no pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring or transport. EMT adds pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring, oral glucose, aspirin, the patient's own nitroglycerin, an inhaled bronchodilator, CPAP, the epinephrine auto-injector. AEMT adds IV and IO access, non-medicated IV fluids, supraglottic airways, waveform capnography, sublingual nitroglycerin and a limited list of IV and IM drugs (dextrose, naloxone). Paramedic adds 12-lead interpretation, manual defibrillation, synchronized cardioversion, transcutaneous pacing, needle chest decompression, intubation and medicated infusions. No newer model was found on 2026-11-17.
The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles.

brief.situation: 19:05. You are a paramedic with an EMT partner. Lena, 58, called with a racing heart for an hour; now she feels faint and has chest tightness.
handover: You carry a monitor-defibrillator with synchronized cardioversion and pacing, adenosine 6 mg/2 mL, IV supplies and the agency's procedural sedation protocol.
The emergency department is 15 minutes away.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated seconds per real second. Pause any time.
Every assessment and treatment takes the time it would on a real call. Scene time and the drive run on the clock.
Partway through you are asked to explain your decisions in writing. The case ends when care is handed over, then a debrief scores what you did.

safetyNote: Teaching case for exam practice; fictional patient. Not medical advice; follow your local protocols and medical direction.

why.question: Explain how you decided this was unstable, why you chose what you did first, and how you checked it worked.

parts.label: Unstable
parts.criteria: A tachyarrhythmia causing hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock and ischemic chest discomfort is unstable (AHA): synchronized cardioversion, not a stable-pathway workup.
parts.modelAnswer: 196 and regular with a pressure near 80, confusion, shock and chest tightness: unstable on every count, so synchronized cardioversion was the priority.

parts.label: Prioritize and act
parts.criteria: Pads, SYNC on and checked, the device's recommended energy, sedation when feasible without delaying; adenosine may be considered for a regular narrow rhythm only if it does not delay the shock; vagal maneuvers are for stable patients; never an unsynchronized shock for a rhythm with a pulse.
parts.modelAnswer: Pads, SYNC confirmed on every QRS, sedation because the IV was in and it cost little time, then the shock at the device's energy. Adenosine only if the shock would be delayed; no Valsalva in someone this sick.

parts.label: Evaluate
parts.criteria: Rhythm, pulse, pressure and mental status after the shock; a 12-lead; reassess on the way.
parts.modelAnswer: Sinus at 98, pressure back to 112, talking again; a 12-lead and repeat checks en route.

expertPath.text: Pale, confused, chest tightness, weak pulse; monitor: narrow regular 196; BP about 80: unstable.
Pads, IV, SYNC on and checked; sedation per protocol.
Synchronized shock: sinus 98. Pressure, 12-lead, load, notify.

converted.headline: Unstable means cardioversion
converted.body: Hypotension, confusion, shock signs and chest discomfort: pads, SYNC, sedation if it didn't delay, shock, then reassess.

arrived.headline: Converted, by a slower route
arrived.body: Time spent on a Valsalva or repeated adenosine let her pressure keep falling.

vf.headline: Sync, or too long
vf.body: An unsynchronized shock can land on the T wave; waiting too long lets the pressure fall until the pulse goes.

scoring.modelReasoning: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 196 with hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock and ischemic chest discomfort is unstable (AHA): synchronized cardioversion at the device's recommended energy, with sedation whenever feasible. Adenosine 6 mg then 12 mg rapid IV may be considered for a regular narrow rhythm only if it does not delay the shock; vagal maneuvers belong to the stable pathway. Confirm SYNC markers on every QRS; never shock unsynchronized with a pulse. Evaluate: rhythm, pressure, mental status, a 12-lead, reassess en route and notify.

unst.ask: While the IV goes in: which finding makes this tachycardia unstable?

choices.label: Her low pressure, confusion and chest tightness

unst.explain: AHA 2025: instability means the tachyarrhythmia is causing hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort or acute heart failure; then synchronized cardioversion.
